sick units in the State and pro-active role played by it to provide financial and technical assistance to them. The
Committee hopes that these efforts will help a lot in improving the condition of sick units in Kerala.
STATE GOVERNMENT SUPPORT TO KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES SECTOR
4.5       The State Government extends 10% rebate on retail sale of Khadi throughout the year. It purchases 75% of the
total requirements of file boards and exempted 23 industries from sales tax. The State Government purchases bandage
cloth for the use of hospitals from the Khadi and Handloom Sectors in the ratio 1 : 1. State Government has also
introduced Incentive Scheme @ Ps. 10 per hank to khadi artisans and extends financial assistance under Plan for the
Khadi Sector.
WELFARE  MEASURES  UNDER  KHADI  SECTOR
4.6       The State Government has constituted a separate body viz. Kerala Khadi Workers Welfare Fund Board for the
welfare of Khadi workers. The following benefits are extended to the Khadi workers by the Welfare Fund Board.
BENEFITS
            1.         Pension to khadi artisans with a minimum of Rs. 100/- and a maximum of Rs. 300/- per month on
completion of 10 years of service or 60 years of age.
            2.         Medical assistance up to Rs. 750/- to an artisan to his/her dependent every year.
            3.         Maternity allowance of Rs. 750/- is given at the time of delivery, limited to times.
            4.         Educational benefit of Rs. 500/- for the children of an artisan for education after SSLC.
            5.         Educational benefit of Rs. 3000/- for courses such as engineering/medicine/ veterinary/agriculture to the
children of artisans.
            6.         Educational cash awards to the toppers among the children of khadi workers at district level.
                                    SSLC   Rs. 1000/-, Rs. 750/-
                                    PDC/Plus2       Rs. 1500/-, Rs. 1000
            7.         Funeral expense @ Rs. 500/- at the time of death of an artisan or dependent.
            8.         Permission to withdraw 50% of the deposited amount for purposes such as house construction,
maintenance, purchase of land or vehicle, marriage of artisan/dependent.
            9.         Interest @ 9.5% to the welfare fund deposit.
4.7       The Committee observes that Kerala is a leading State in the welfare measures for khadi artisans. The
State Khadi Workers' Welfare Fund is a model to be examined by other States for implementation. The State
Government gives support to the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board by providing substantial funds
under plan fund in addition to non-plan funds for salary and rebate. A rebate of 10% on the sale of khadi is
available throughout the year. The State Government has introduced an incentive scheme to the khadi artisans
@ 10 paisa per hank in weaving. Further, the State Government has reserved a portion of Khadi materials for
the requirement of hospital to be procured from the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board. The Committee
appreciates and recognizes the efforts of the State Government in extending support to Khadi and Village Sector.
MARKETING
4.8       The Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board is running 163 numbers of sales outlets. A considerable quantity
of Khadi and Village Industries products produced by the Board and its aided units are being sold out through these
outlets. Nowadays, Board is giving particular attention in opening more sales outlets under the direct control of the
Board. The objective behind this is to dispose of the heavy accumulation of Khadi goods turned out in the production
centres.
4.9       Out of the above, 9 sales outlets are run by the Director (Marketing) directly. In addition to this, the Project
Officers are also running 20 of Khadi Grama Soubhagyas in all districts. There are 49 agency Bhavans and 84 numbers
of Grama Soubhagyas attached to the production units. The total sales achieved during 2001-2002 from all the Grama
Soubhagyas is Rs. 847.90 lakhs.
4.10     The Board has launched two types of readymade shirts with the brand name 'Summer cool' and 'Millenti'. It has
great demand in Kerala. The Board is also thinking of supplying the products to other State Boards. Similarly the Board

has a brand new product of honey named 'Naruthen'. The Board is thinking of exporting their brand products to outside
the country, especially to the Middle East. A focal point will be set up in the Khadi and Village Industries Board shortly
to explore possibilities of exporting Khadi and Village Industries products.
4.11     The Committee observes that the major concern in the field of marketing of Khadi products is the rebate
policy of KVIC. The Committee hopes that the KVIC will announce its policy on time.
4.12     In the budget estimate for 2002-03 KVIC was requested to allot Rs. 40 lakhs for exhibition and Rs. 60 lakhs for

4.13     The Committee recommends that the funds demanded in the budget proposal for the above items for
2002-03 may be considered sympathetically.

4.14     The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) has set up a Central Silver Plant (Muslin Project) at
Kuttur, near Trichur for ensuring supply of silver/roving to the institutions of this State. The centre caters to the need of
silver/roving to the institutions of West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, U.P., Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat also. The
total supply of roving within the State comes to around 2 lakh kgs., and that of outside the State comes to 1.40 lakh kgs.
During 2001-02, the production of the unit was 3.69 lakh kgs. worth Rs. 441.00 lakhs. The actual sale was to the tune of
3.40 lakh kgs. for an amount of Rs. 419.00 lakhs. The accrued profit as on 31.3.2002 is to the extent of Rs. 176.15 lakhs.
The total investment of the plant and machinery of the unit is Rs. 166.18 lakhs. The silver/roving is being supplied to
the institutions on credit against the rebate payment so that the working capital is not blocked and ensured continued
production.
4.15     The Committee observes that Kerala being a consumer State more silver plants on the pattern of Central
Siler Plants, Kuttur, Trichur should be set up so that demands of the State of Khadi Products can be met.
BIO-TECHNOLOGY/NON-CONVENTIONAL  ENERGY  PROGRAMME
4.16     "Bio-technology and Non-conventional Energy" is one of the major industries functioning in Kerala. Various

30-60 rural unemployed artisans. The subsidy rates varies from Rs. 1800/- to Rs. 2300/- per biogas plant and

4.17     KVIC is also engaged in development of "bio-manure". KVIC is extending technical expertise in disseminating
various bio-manure techniques, bio-digested slurry etc. besides financial assistance under the scheme. So far half a
dozen units have been installed and a good number of units are under different stages of installation.
4.18     The Committee appreciates the efforts of Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board in developing bio-
technology/non-conventional energy programme. The Committee hopes that action will be taken to install more
such units in the State.
RURAL  EMPLOYMENT  GENERATION  PROGRAMME  (REGP)
4.19     The REGP is being implemented in the State, with the active involvement of the State KVI Board and Public
Sector Scheduled Commercial Banks. So far, 5246 Village Industries Projects have been set up in the State under the
programme.

4.20     The State KVI Board aided agencies are actively involved in the implementation of REGP. KVIC has placed Rs.
14.19 crore Margin Money advance with the State KVI Board for speedy implementation of the programme. The Board
has already sanctioned and released Margin Money Assistance to the tune of Rs. 14.18 crore to 1403 Village Industries
Units generating employment opportunity to 11844 persons in rural sector. The Board is providing Margin Money
Assistance to all industries included under the schedule of industries approved by Khadi and Village Industries
Commission.

specific objective of giving fillip to an IT based endeavour for rural development. The Board also proposes to impart a
short-term training to the prospective entrepreneurs in this regard.

Government to tap the inherent skills of the rural populace and transform them into economic assets for self-

employment and higher earnings.

            The Committee observes that in order to identify the drawbacks in the functioning of the Khadi institutions and

these programmes in the State on priority basis and realize their fullest potential. NGOs may also be invited and
encouraged to popularize these programmes.    (Para 2.11)

THIRTEENTH  MEETING
            The Committee met at 3.30 p.m. on Wednesday, the 11th December, 2002 in Room No. 62, First Floor,
Parliament House, New Delhi.
            1.         Dr. P.C. Alexander  —  Chairman
                        RAJYA  SABHA
            2.         Prof. M.M. Agarwal

2.         At the outset the Chairman welcomed the Members and apprised them of agenda for the meeting 
of the day.
3.         The Committee thereafter, took up auto policy for discussion. The Chairman apprised the Members that the
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry had recommended in its 59th Report that the Government should
formulate an Auto Policy in view of the ongoing liberalization of the economy and W.T.O. Obligations. In response to
the Committee's recommendations the Department of Heavy Industries in its Action Taken Note has informed the
Committee that Government of India has brought out an Auto Policy on 7th March, 2002.
3.1       The Chairman stated that the Committee on Industry took up the auto policy for detailed discussion as the policy
laid down certain recommendations for the growth of the Industry. Since most of these recommendations required
actions by the Ministries other than the Department of Heavy Industries and so far these recommendations had not been
translated into real Government Policy.
3.2.      The Chairman apprised the Members that the Committee had already taken up the matter for discussion and in
this regard the Committee had held two meetings on 24th June and 16th July, 2002. Based on the discussion held on
24th June, 2002 a questionnaire was prepared and replies thereon was obtained from Department of Heavy Industries. In
the meeting held on 16th July, 2002 the Committee had interacted with Automotive Research Association of India
(ARAI); Society of India Automobiles Manufacturers (SIAM); Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association (ATMA);
and Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA); Prozon Inc. (manufacture of Fuel saver). Apprising
the Members the details of discussion held in these two meetings, the Chairman spelt out the scope for discussion in
auto policy which inter-alia included import of second hand imported cars; lack of testing facilities; foreign direct
investment, research and development; construction of bus-body building, terminal life policy, lifting of quantitative
restriction; Using spurious items and related 'e' mark issue; excise duty on tyre and concession on import tyre; Ban on
used tyre; difficulties due to octroi on 5-6 States, switching over from Tube tyre to tubeless tyre; encouragement to
small car industries; infrastructure import tariff; environmental aspects etc.
3.3       The Committee, thereafter, discussed in details the aims of Auto Policy which aimed at to promote integrated,
phased, enduring and self-sustained growth of the Indian Automobile Industry. The Committee discussed also the
objective of Auto Policy which inter-alia include promotion of a globally competitive automotive industry; Exalting the
sector as a lever of industrial growth and an employment; Establishment of an international hub for manufacturing small
affordable passenger cars and key centre for manufacturing Tractors and Two wheelers in the world; Ensuing a balanced
transition to open trade at a minimal risk to the Indian Economy and local industry; Modernisation of the industry by
facilitating indigenous design, research and development; Steering up India's software industry into automotive

technology; Development of domestic safety and environmental standard at par with international standards; assisting
development of vehicles propelled by alternative energy sources.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised by the
Committee, hereby present this Ninety-seventh Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on Demands for Grants for (2002-03) pertaining to
the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.
2.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report at its meeting held
on the 11th December, 2002.
3.      The 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid
on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
11 December, 2002
NEW DELHI;
Dr.  P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
        The Ninety-seventh Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in
the 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on the Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the
14th May, 2002.
2.     Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. They have
been categorized as follows:
(i)    Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:- Paras: 3.24, 3.27, 3.28, 3.30, 3.32, 3.35, 3.36,
3.41, 4.2, 4.3, 5.5, 5.6, 5.9, 5.11, 6.9, 6.10, 6.12, 6.13, 6.14, 6.15 (Chapter-I).
(ii)    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies: - Paras :
1.2, 3.2, 3.37, 6.1, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5 (Chapter - II).
(iii)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Government: - Paras: 3.9,
3.10, 3.12, 3.15, 6.6, 6.7, 7.5 (Chapter - III).
(iv)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been received: - Paras: 3.13,
3.20, 3.21, 3.22, 3.42, 6.16, 6.17 (Chapter - IV).
(v)   Observations/Recommendations at a Glance (Chapter - V).
3.     The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has accepted its recommendations as mentioned
in Chapter-I of the Report.
4.     In respect of the recommendations made in Chapter-II the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation advocated by the
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries and therefore does not want to pursue further.
5.     The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations of Recommendations contained in Chapter-III and therefore the
Committee desires that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
6.     In respect of Recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has either furnished the interim
replies or couched its language in vague terms like the Ministry's views have been conveyed to concerned agencies, therefore, the
Committee desires that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would furnish Action Taken Note in respects of recommendations
categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
7.     The details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
Internal Resource Generation by KVIC
Para 3.24
        The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should take steps to generate internal resources on its own so as to reduce the
dependence on budgetary resources of the Government as far as possible, by evolving suitable mechanisms like revamping of KVIC
staff, aggressive marketing of KVI products, brand building and other measures so that it becomes self-sufficient and self-reliant. A long-
term strategy for suitable positioning of Khadi for the next 5-10 years needs to be prepared, otherwise the very survival of KVIC as an
institution would be in doubt.
Comments
        The suggestions made have been noted and communicated to the KVIC for taking further necessary action.
Unspent Balance of KVIC
Para 3.27
        The Committee views with concern that KVIC had an unspent balance of Rs. 147.51 crore as on 31st March, 2001. This is not a
healthy trend, as non-utilisation of money earmarked for a specific purpose does not augur well for the premier institution. The money
should have been put to better use.
Comments
        The point suggested has been noted and communicated to the KVIC for strict compliance.
Budget Management by KVIC
Para 3.28
        The Committee recommends that in cases where lapses had been continuing over the years, responsibility should be fixed and better
budget management undertaken. This would be a major step forward. The Committee recommends further that expenditure framework
needs to be strengthened. This would involve identifying current and future financial requirements, and deviations from the prescribed
procedure should not be allowed under any circumstances.
Comments
        Suggestions made have been noted and communicated to the KVIC for strict compliance.
Non-Plan Expenditure of KVIC
Para 3.30
        The Committee finds that non-plan allocation for Khadi and Village Industries shows an increasing trend. It is also not managed
efficiently while KVIC is over-staffed. The Committee recommends that KVIC should undertake trimming exercise for reducing surplus
staff by extending VRS in order to curtail non-plan expenditure and to make the institution economically viable.
Comments:
        The suggestions made has been noted and communicated to the KVIC for further necessary action However, it may be clarified that
the expenditure under non-plan has increased to meet expenditure against salary and wages for which adequate provision did not exist
earlier. The expenditure earlier was being met through diversion of other funds/earnings.
Report of Arther Andersen on KVIC
Para 3.32
        The Committee observes that the report of Arthur Andersen was submitted in September, 2000 and is still under examination by the
KVIC. The Committee recommends that the examination of the report be expedited and a final view be taken without further delay.
Comments
        The direction has been noted.
Inventory
Paras 3.35 and 3.36

3.35 The Committee expresses serious concern that the stocks of goods worth several hundred crores are lying locked and unused.
Perhaps this is why, KVIC has been experiencing working capital difficulties. If this state of affairs continues, KVIC will not only be
faced with resource crunch as the money remains locked up and stocks lying unsold but also lose customer base as there will be no takers
for the old stocks.
Comments
        The continuous efforts are being made to liquidate stocks which have reduced from Rs. 658 crores approximately in March, 2001 to
Rs. 579 crores in March, 2002.
3.36 The Committee recommends that KVIC should dispose of the old stock as early as possible even by providing heavy discounts and
recover money. KVIC may utilize the revenue earned on fresh inventory and recycle the money. KVIC should keep fresh inventory as
old inventory would not fetch much money.
Comments
        Rebate policy for the year 2002-03 has been announced. KVIC has been directed to take urgent remedial action to see that old stock
lying in the various godowns of KVIC and that of Khadi Institutions is reduced to minimum.
Review of stock build-up
Para 3.41
        The Committee recommends that CCPC should henceforth undertake periodical review of the stock build-up before approving the
quantities to be purchased. Further, responsibility for the lapses for allocating of funds and excess stocking of cotton on the part of
officials/non-officials should be fixed.
Comments
        The suggestion of the Committee has been noted and has already been communicated to KVIC for taking further necessary action.
Ministry has already asked KVIC to fix the responsibility for the lapses for allocating of funds and excess stocking of cotton on the
defaulting officials.
Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC)
Paras 4.2 & 4.3
4.2   The Committee observes that in spite of KVIC's repeated request over the years, funds flow to KVI institutions from banks under
ISEC is not up to the desired level. Analysis of ISECs issued by KVIC and actual funds made available by banks against the ISEC
indicates that in the recent past the gap in the ISEC value vis-a-vis fund provided by banks goes to be extent of 50%.
Comments
        The Ministry is in agreement with the observations of the Committee. Necessary action is being taken in this matter.
4.3   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India/RBI may take appropriate policy decision so that banks are
bound to honour the ISECs issued by the KVIC to its full extent.
Comments
        The matter has been taken up with the banks by the Ministry so that the recommendations of the Committee will be implemented by
KVIC and banks.
EXIM Policy - 2002
Para 5.5
        The five year EXIM policy announced on 1st April, 2002 seeks to enable Indian artisans, Cottage and Small Industries to venture
out overseas and adopt the world as their market. The new policy makes exports free, easy and possibly rewarding. This assumes special
significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given global slowdown and domestic recession. The EXIM policy is
comprehensive, encompassing agro sector, cottage and handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% of the
population living in rural areas.
Comments
        A draft scheme for export promotion of KVI products under the EXIM policy has been formulated which has been sent for vetting to
Finance Wing. It will be implemented very shortly.
Coir Products

Para 5.6
        The Committee therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms of coir products and product
mix should be attempted. Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for improving the quality of the coir fibre, for
enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced in non traditional coir producing areas using "coirret". The
Committee also notes that the market for coir pith, a waste material of the coir industry converted into one of major export items in the
list of coir products, remains untapped and the potential for the export of coir pith is excellent. The Committee therefore, recommends
that all out efforts should be made to make pith export achieve its fullest potential.
Comments
        The recommendations have been noted for further action. However, in this connection it is stated that under the UNDP assisted
project, the Coir Board has entered into a collaborative project with the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad for stratetgic Design
Intervention and product development for diversification of coir industry. As a part of this project blending coir with other natural fibres
like sisal, jute, banana, rami etc. and spin finer count yarn for making innovative products like vertical blinds, curtain materials etc. has
been undertaken. The Coir Board has already conducted workshops for training the representatives of the trade for blending coir fibre
with other natural fibres and to manufacture value added products out of it. For diversification of coir products, a project has been
undertaken in association with Indian Institute of Packaging, Mumbai for developing package material using coir fibre.
        As recommended by the Committee, the Board is taking efforts in association with the private sector for promoting export of coir
pith. Besides, the Coir Board has developed a fungal spawn viz. Pith Plus for converting coir pith into organic manure. The technology
for production of Coir Pith Organic Manure (C-POM) using Pith Plus is being popularized in the trade by organizing field demonstrations
in the selected coir production centers as a continuing plan programme. The Coir Board extends financial assistance to the entrepreneurs
for setting up coir pith processing units for which assistance to the tune of 25% of the capital investment on work shed and equipment
would be provided by the Coir Board subject to a ceiling of Rs. 1,00,000/-. These programmes are proposed to be continued during the
Tenth Plan period also.
Allocation Offund for Coir
Para 5.9
        The Committee observes that coir sector employs 5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its activities. Although the
funds allocation for the sector has been doubled in the Ninth Five Year Plan from what it was in the Eighth Five Year Plan, (Rs. 31 crores
during the Eighth Five Year Plan and Rs. 60 crores during the Ninth Five Year Plan), this sector is still under budgeted. There is further
scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh,
Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new products could be developed. The Committee therefore recommends that
the allocation for the coir industry should be revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this
sector.
Comments
        Against the Plan allocation of Rs.31.00 crores during the Eighth Five Year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the Ninth Five Year Plan, a
higher allocation of Rs.115 crores has been made for the coir sector during the Tenth Five Year Plan.
Welfare Measures in Coir Industry
Para 5.11
        The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare for the people, especially women, engaged in the coir industry which remains
unorganized to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives would be taken in near future for the benefit of large
number of people engaged in the industry.
Comments
        The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future guidance.
Recovery Under PMRY
Para 6.9
        The Committee observes that the crux of the problem lies in the recovery scenario under PMRY which has been showing a
decreasing trend. If this sort of thing continues, there will be less funds available year by year to channelise for future schemes as the
money will be in short supply. A stage may come that the scheme may have to be closed down due to non-availability of funds. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that recovery of loans, which is a grey area in the present scenario, should be given more attention
and loopholes in this regard should be plugged so that the scheme may not be scuttled for want of funds in future and recycling of funds
may continue. The Chairman/Managing Directors - All India Scheduled Commercial Banks may be suitably advised by the RBI to

improve their recovery performance to recycle the funds and constitute recovery cells at Regional/Zonal Office level.
Comments
        The Chairman/Managing Directors, all Indian Scheduled Commercial Banks have been suitably advised by the RBI to improve the
recovery performance to re-cycle the funds and constitute 'Recovery Cell' and Regional/controlling office level, to improve further by
their Circular No. RPCD.SP.BC. 13/09.04.01/2000-01 dated 04.09.2000. On the advice of the RBI, Union Bank of India, Central Bank of
India, Dena Bank and Bank of India have constituted 'Recovery Cells' at Regional/Zonal Office levels. The RBI has further advised
banks to keep a close watch on the recovery of loan through better post-disbursement credit supervision vide  their Letter No.
RPCD.SP.BC. 34/09.04.01/2001-02 dated 19.10.2001. As per the report received from the RBI, the recovery for half year ending Sept.,
2001 has slightly improved and is 28.8 for the half year ending Sept., 2001. However, the observation of the Committee under Para 6.9
have again been communicated to the RBI for taking further necessary action vide Letter No. PMRY-P/PC/10(1)/2002 deted 16.07.02.
Achievement of Target under PMRY
Paras 6.10, 6.11, 6.12, and 6.13
6.10 The Committee futher observes that though the Government achieved in some measure quantitative target of the PMRY, no efforts
were made either by the Government or by other agencies to evaluate the qualitative achievement of the scheme. The beneficiaries
experienced difficulties in starting and running the venture. The major problem in starting the unit was in getting the loan. 50% of the
beneficiaries were affected by the delay in disbursement of the loan. This forced them to take loan from moneylenders at a very high rate
of interest and this had an adverse effect on their business. The beneficiaries reported that because of the financial delay they could not
reach their expectations. The beneficiaries of the category made default in payment of loan.
6.11 The Committee finds that shortage of funds for working capital is hindering the PMRY beneficiaries. They could not execute their
orders in time due to shortage of funds and for marketing capital requirements, they resort to private money lenders at a high rate of
interest resulting in the increased cost of production and short fall in profit margin.
6.12 The high cost of operation is another problem where 20% of the industries were affected by this and they could not compete in the
local market. Increase in the cost of spare parts are the main cost accelerating items and entrepreneurs could not repay the interest in time.
The entrepreneurs could not adjust themselves to the demand and supply mechanism of the market.
6.13 As regards the undue delay in giving loans by banks, the Committee impresses upon banks to avoid undue delay. The Committee
recommends that implementing banks should be advised by the RBI to sanction the applications within the prescribed time frame and
speedily dispose off the same to ensure that there is no inordinate gap between the sanction and disbursement of loan. DICs should play a
pro-active role in this regard. RBI's guidelines for disposing of applications under PMRY within the time period of thirty days must be
adhered to by banks.
Comments
        Banks have been advised by the RBI to dispose off applications upto a credit limit of Rs.25,000 within a fortnight and those for over
Rs.25,000/- within a 8-9 weeks vide  their Letter No. RPCD.SP.BC.303/09.04.01/1994-95 dated 1.8.94. The implementing banks have
been advised by the RBI to sanction the application within the prescribed time frame and speedily dispose off the same to ensure that
there is no inordinate gap between sanction and disbursement of loan vide  their Letter No. RPCD.SP.BC.34/09.04.01/1994-45 dated
19.10.01. The recommendations of the Committee as contained in its 74th Report have also been communicated to the RBI and to the
States/UTs vide Letter No. PMRY-P-PC/10(1)/2002 dated 16.07.02.
Power Connection under PMRY
Para 6.14
        Delay in getting power connection affected 30% of them in terms of production and marketing. Delay in getting delivery of assets
forced them to postpone the launch of their project eventually leading to addition to cost of the project. This upsets the success of the
project and may lead to more defaulters in future. Delay in power connection/power cut also affected their production and resulted in the
increased cost of production.
6.15 As regards, the delay in getting power connection, the Committee desires that Government should take suitable action in the matter
and impress upon the State Governments to deal such cases on priority basis.
Comments
        The observations of the Committee have been communicated to States/UTs vide this Office Letter No. PMRY-P/PC/10(1)/2002
dated 17.7.02

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF
THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
Para 1.2
        The Committee welcomes the formation of the new Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. It has satisfied the long-felt need for the
creation of a new Ministry which would look exclusively after the needs of this sector. This is expected to give a boost to the sector,
especially when our industries now face competition from global companies and find it hard to survive.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Constitution of KVIC
Para 3.2
        The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 49th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro and Rural Industries had expressed its concern at the inordinate delay in
reconstituting the Khadi and Village Industries Commission. The term of the previous Khadi and Village Industries Commission expired
in September, 1999 and since then the Commission had been non-existent which adversely affected the working of Khadi and Village
Industries. The Committee has been informed that the Commission has been reconstituted w.e.f. 2nd October, 2001. The Committee
welcomes the reconstitution of the Commission and hopes that the new Commission will be able to take care of the requirements of the
Khadi sector to make it self sustaining and vibrant.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Poor Quality and Design of Khadi Products
Para 3.37
        The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of large inventories. The
working cycle of production sales-cash-realization for Khadi is long and substantial funds are blocked as working capital for Khadi
institutions. This has adversely affected performance.
Comments
        The slump in Khadi performance was mainly attributed to the production of goods, which are not as per demand and taste of the
market. It was a fact that most of the Khadi producing institutions located in rural areas could not cope up with fast changing consumer
tastes particularly in cotton textile materials. This has to a large extent, resulted in the accumulation of inventory. One of the important
requirements in the above backdrop is the improvement in the quality and design of Khadi products. The Government of India is
implementing the Khadi package for Khadi and Village Industries programme which envisages better design development, quality
assurance standards etc. On implementation of such measures it is expected that the performance of Khadi sector would improve
considerably.
Employment Generation Under PMRY
Para 6.1
        The PMRY has emerged as a major Central Sector Scheme for employment generation among the educated unemployed youth, by
providing financial and other entrepreneurial development assistance in establishing self-employment ventures. Significant progress has
been achieved in the implementation of the scheme and as reported by the RBI, 7.748 lakh persons have been sanctioned loans under
PMRY, since its inception during the 8th Five Year Plan. The scheme is continuing in the 9th Five Year Plan. During the years 1997-98,
1998-99, 1999-2000 and 2000-01 loans have been sanctioned to 10.20 lakh persons. Further, 0.48 lakh persons have been sanctioned
loans during 2001-02 upto November, 2001. The anticipated target PMRY for 2002-03 is 2.2 lakh beneficiaries. The entrepreneurs
sanctioned loan under the scheme are provided stipendiary entrepreneurship, development training by various training institutions. The
period of training for industry sector is 5-20 working days and for service/business sector 7 to 10 working days. The training expenditure
admissible including stipend for industry sector is upto Rs.1,000/- per trainee and for service/business sector upto Rs.500/- per trainee.
The Central Government provides funds for training of beneficiaries and other entrepreneurial development activities in the form of
subsidy @ 5 per cent of project cost subject to a ceiling of Rs.15,000/- per beneficiary in respect of North Easterm States and Rs.7,500/-
per beneficiary for rest of the country. Besides this, funds are provided to the States/UTs for scheme operation.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT
BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE
Wardha Institute
Para 3.9
        The Committee welcomes this move as it aught to provide a great fillip to the sector. Simultaneously, the Committee notes that there
is no specific provision in the Budget for the required funds to implement the announcement of upgrading the Wardha Institute as a
National Institute named after Mahatma Gandhi. The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need for additional provision of at least
Rs.100 crores for the Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialisation, Wardha. This provision may be spread over a period of three
years.
Comments
        The Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Mumbai (KVIC), a statutory body under the administrative control of the Ministry of
Agro and Rural Industries has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the IIT, Delhi in April, 2001 to implement a
three-year Project for revamping of the existing Jamnalal Bajaj Central Research Institute (JBCRI), Wardha and convert it into Mahatma
Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI). The duration of the Project is 3 years (May-2001 - April-2004). The total allocation
for the project is Rs. 8.35 crores. A total of Rs. 5.70 crores has so far been released to the KVIC under S&T including funds for the
implementation of this Project and the balance will be released in due course during the project period. It is hoped that the project will be
completed during the stipulated time-frame and within the total project outlay. There has not been any project cost revision-requiring
provision of Rs.100 crores. The project implementation is constantly under review to ensure that there are no slippages in the completion
of the project.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        Since this is an important national project, the Committee feels that it should be completed by April, 2004. The Committee
impresses upon the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries to keep on vigil on the progress of the project.
R&D for KVIC
Para 3.10
        The Committee observes that R&D is the need of the hour if industries are to compete globally and growth in the sector is to be
stimulated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation for Research and Development for KVIC requires be increased. If
need be, joint collaboration with foreign firms may to be taken up.
Comments
        The Ministry is alive to the significance of R&D to promote global competitiveness of the indigenous industries. Therefore,
Government in its effort to strengthen Village Industries (VIs) for production of quality marketable goods, has been making substantial
funding to help organizations and entrepreneurs to promote their existing sphere of activities. But very little investment has gone into
research and development of support services infrastructure to promote and disseminate improved technology to increase productivity
and quality standards of goods produced in rural areas by the Village Industries.
        The inputs of S&T for Technology Upgradation, transfer of appropriate technology, quality assessment of associated inputs, Quality
Control/Assurance Mechanism of final products are some of the important areas where organizations like Khadi and Village Industries
Commission (KVIC), Mumbai under this Ministry, could play an important role either through its own infrastructure or using
infrastructure available elsewhere for the strengthening of Rural Industrialisation.
        In order to provide such inputs to the Village Industries sector in the country, Government has approved the following as part of the
Khadi Package announced in May, 2001:-
A.    Strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC.
B.     To establish technical inter faces with the technical establishments in the country.
C.    Networking of Quality Testing/Certifying laboratories/Institutions in the country.
        Institutions have been selected by the Government for upgrading R&D facilities. As per the package announced by the Government

97th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/97threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:53]
of India, funds allotted under sector specific R&D will be utilized to the tune of Rs. 1550 lakhs over a three years period.
        Similarly, Technical Back-up Units (TBUs/Interfaces) covering the entire country at some S&T institutes will be set up. All these
units will form a network. The proposed Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation at Wardha will be the main node of this
network.
        In order to strengthen the quality assurance labs, the KVIC will enter into MoUs with existing laboratories recognized by the
National Accredition Board for Laboratories (NABL) which will cover both the public sector as well as private sector. KVIC products
will be standard sized according to BIS/AGMARK/FPO/ etc. Adequate budget provision will be made for strengthening of the quality
control laboratories.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC was announced in May, 2001 but not much progress
has been made in the matter. The Committee recommends that this project should be completed in a definite time-frame.
JPRGY
Para 3.12
        While appreciating this initiative, the Committee expresses its concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of NPRI (National
Programme for Rural Industrialisation as announced in the Budget for the financial year 1999-2000. The allocation of Rs.40 lakhs was
kept for the NPRI scheme in the BE 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal amount of Rs.1.00 lakh in the RE of that year. The scheme is
yet to take off. However, in the BE  2002-03 a provision of Rs. 90 lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore impresses upon the
Ministry to review the progress of NPRI so that the earlier mistakes are not repeated by the administration.
Comments
        The scheme on NPRI was announced in the year 1999-2000 with a mission to set up 100 rural clusters every year. Office of the DC
(SSI) was made the coordinating agency of the programme. KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD are the major implementing agencies. No fund
was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own programmes in this
area which could be coordinated and their synergies exploited for better impact.
        Efforts were made to firm up the scheme at the initial stage. A number of meetings were called in which all the agencies involved in
rural industrialization participated. A national level Steering Committee was constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (SSI &
ARI) to guide, implement and monitor the programme. Consequently, KVIC identified 50 clusters for development for each year, SIDBI
25 and NABARD 50 for a period of 5 years. So far, KVIC has launched the programme in 20 clusters, NABARD in 14 and SIDBI in 13.
The other clusters are also under consideration and preliminary/diagnostic studies are being conducted of these clusters. It was, however,
felt that some fund was required for certain gap filling exercises towards cluster intervention. Therefore, the Office of the DC (SSI)
launched a scheme on NPRI in the year 2001-02 to supplement the efforts of the various agencies. The amount provided in the scheme is
only Rs.5 lakhs per cluster. The purpose of financial assistance is to fill certain gaps in the development of clusters, and it does not
constitute the entire amount required for such development. As the scheme has been approved in the year 2001-02, it is expected to yield
results in the coming years.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee fails to understand as to why a scheme is announced by the Government without any budgetary provision. Ministry's
reply that no fund was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordinated and their synergy exploited for their impact does not appear to be sound because this
Committee has its own experience that coordination among Central Ministries and Departments is a difficult preposition to achieve. The
Committee now expects that with the provision of funds the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would implement the programme.
Increasing the Sales of Khadi
Para 3.15
        The Committee feels that for increasing sales of Khadi and providing greater and better rural employment opportunities in this
sector, it is necessary to provide and offer products that match consumer preferences.
Comments
        The Ministry is in total agreement with the observations of the Committee.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee feels that action oriented proposals should be mooted by the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries in this
regard.

Para 7.5
        The Committee welcomes the increase in the allocation for creating additional employment opportunities under REGP. The
programme can prove to be a major instrument in bringing about self-sufficiency for rural populace and in getting rid of unemployment
problems in a big way, if implemented by State KVI Boards in an effective manner. In order to implement the REGP/Margin Money
Scheme, KVIC has also placed Margin Money Grant with State/UT/KVI Boards in advance, so that the programme can be implemented
without any delay. However, the Committee observes that due to weak infrastructure facilities some of the State/UT/KVI Boards are not
in a position to utilize such grants made available to them even after a lapse of considerable time. The Committee therefore recommends
that KVIC should impress upon State Governments to strengthen State KVI Boards by providing adequate technical experts and other
necessary infrastructure facilities like training, R&D etc. so that REGP scheme may be implemented successfully.
Comments
        The position of utilization under REGP has improved considerably during the past 2 years. For instance margin money utilization by
bank has gone up from Rs. 53.34 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs.149.84 crores in 2001-02. Similarly margin money utilization by KVIBs has
gone up from Rs.24.39 crores to Rs.40.41 crores during same period. However suggestion of the Committee for strengthening State
KVIBs is noted and will be communicated to the State Governments.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee recommends that KVIC should help State KVIs to build adequate infrastructure to implement more projects as State
KVICs find themselves helpless in implementing of projects in the absence of adequate infrastructure.

            Under the National Mineral Policy, 1993, 13 minerals hitherto reserved for exploitation by Public Sector were
thrown open for exploitation by Private Sector also and thereby provided a level playing field to private companies in

resulting in expected FDI inflow of Rs.3963 crores.  The National Mineral Policy, 1993 has also recognized the need for

contributed towards national exchequer and society in general.  Besides this, a number of amendments have been carried
out in the MMDR Act, 1957, MCR, 1960 and MCDR, 1988,  since 1994 to make Indian mining sector investor friendly

Action Taken:
 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993, recognised the need for encouraging private investment including foreign
direct investment and state-of-the-art technology in mineral sector. Further , National Mineral Policy 1993 has  stressed 
that the Central  Government in consultation with the State Governments, shall continue to formulate the legal measures
for the regulation of mines and the development of mineral resources to ensure basic  uniformity  in mineral 
administration and to ensure that the development of mineral resources keeps pace, and is in consonance with the
national policy goals.
 
It is therefore evident that review of the policy and consequent amendment(s) in the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and rules framed there under to cater to future demands is(are)  an ongoing
process, and can not be a one time exercise.
 
 For a structured  and institutionalized review of the policies and procedures affecting the mining and the mineral
sector and for all matters connected or incidental thereto, the Mineral Advisory Council has been constituted by the
Government. The Hon’ble Minister for Coal and Mines is the Chairman of the Council. The Council has balanced
representation from State Governments, Industry Associations , Experts in mining sector as well as Members of
Parliament. The Mineral Advisory Council inter alia reviews the status of implementation of the National Mineral
Policy, advises the Government on mineral policy and legislation and the status of the mining and the mineral sector,
including inter alia  all the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its Report.
 
After the National Mineral Policy was announced, Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
has been amended in 1994 and 1999. After amendment in the Principal Act in 1999, the Mineral Concession Rules,
1960 have been amended on January 17,.2000, September 25,.2000,January 22,2000, and on January 11.,2002 .
Similarly, after 1999, the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules 1988 have been amended on 17.1.2000,
25.9.2000 and 11.1.2002.
The  amendments in the legislation have been extensively discussed prior to their enactment and honed as per
recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council in its various meetings. As a recent example, minerals for which the
State Governments would be empowered to approve mining plans have been identified, time limits have been prescribed
for  conveying a decision on application(s) for mineral concessions and mining plans, and fees payable for various
applications under the rules have been revised as per recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council.
 
            Two meetings of the Mineral Advisory Council have been held since 1999. In addition the Department of Mines
organized a Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology, as well as a Tripartite Meeting of the Central
Government, State Governments and Investors in the Mining Sector in 2001. These meetings also discussed inter alia
the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. The review of the National Mineral Policy
and the other issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee will therefore appropriately be listed for
discussion in the next meeting of the Mineral Advisory Committee.         
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee expects  that the  Department of Mines  understands the concern  of Department related
Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Industry  and  therefore  appreciate its desire accordingly.  Interchanging and
intermingling  and  the functions of  Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee with  Mineral Advisory
Council  would not only be belittling and undermining the status of  this Committee   but also juxtaposing  the role   of
Mineral Advisory Council.    The Department of Mines placed  the issues identified  by the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry in the meetings of  Mineral Advisory Council  but deprived the Committee of the outcome of the
meetings and  discussion held.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should  furnish the details of 
Action Taken in its Note and  apprise the Committee comprehensively.   The Committee recommends that  the
Department of Mines should forward the  minutes of the meeting of Mineral Advisory  Council  to this Committee
whenever  the Mineral Advisory Council discusses the issues identified by the Committee.

FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN MINING SECTOR
 The Committee appreciates  the  efforts made by the Department of Mines towards making the  mining sector more  
investor friendly  but  at the same time hopes that  pace of foreign  investment  in the mining sector may be  
accelerated.
Action Taken:
            The liberalisation of policy has provided a conducive atmosphere for the international mining companies to
invest in the country and bring with this investment and world class mining technology.  The policy of the Government
of India has been to actively encourage foreign investors to participate in the exploration and production of minerals and
mineral based industries.  Sustained inflow of private including foreign investment is desirable to bring in state-of-the-
art technology, coupled with foreign capital for the exploration and exploitation of mineral resources and in-country
value addition.
            As a part of the policy to actively encourage such investments, in order to give a further push for the FIPB
approved projects to get off the ground quickly, a monitoring system has been put in place.  This involves a periodic
review by the Foreign Investment Implementation Authority (FIIA), which looks at the progress made in implementing
the major projects.  Also, within each Ministry, there is a Fast Tract Committee (FTC) which closely monitors the
projects in that particular sector.
            The Department of Mines has been effectively utilizing various international fora, to highlight the policy and
legislative initiatives undertaken to project India as an attractive investment destination and the opportunities available. 
In this context the response has been good.
            Meetings with foreign investors have also been organized to identify the problems in implementation of various
Projects.  A time frame for disposal of applications for mineral concessions have also been fixed in the Mineral
Concession Rules.  These initiatives will accelerate the inflow of foreign investment in the mining sector.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee observes that the Department of Mines have  furnished in its Action Taken Note only the
institutional  arrangement for accelerating  the pace  of foreign investment in the Mining Sector   but that is not
sufficient, the Committee feels.  The  Department of Mines should have furnished the details of  course of action
undertaken to promote foreign investment in the mining sector, region and  mineral-wise  and the outcome of efforts  so
made in the  form of quantum of  foreign investment.  The Committee recommends that FIIA and FTC should play  pro-
active role   for promotion of foreign investment.

CHAPTER-I 
INTRODUCTORY  
 
 
1.1  The Ministry of Labour & Employment is respons ible for 
protecting and safeguarding the interests of worker s, promotion of 
their welfare and providing social security to them both in organized 
and unorganized sectors.  The main objectives of the Ministry are: 
  (i)  To ensure welfare of labourers 
  (ii)  To oversee increase in prosperity 
  (iii) To promote harmonious relations between lab our and  
  management and to regulate wages and other condit ions  
  of work in the central sphere. 
 (iv) To ensure speedy implementation of labour law  awards,  
  agreements, code of discipline etc. for improving    
  industrial relations with regard to units in whic h Central  
  Government is the appropriate Government. 
 (v) To conduct evaluatory studies of implementatio n of   
  labour laws, industrial relations, personnel poli cies and  
  practices etc., in Public Sector Undertakings. 
 (vi) To regulate working conditions and safety in mines and  
  factories. 
 

8 
 
 (vii) To prepare ground work for the formulation o f National  
  Wage Policy and maintain data on wages, all allow ances  
  and other related matters. 
 (viii) To collect and publish statistics to conduc t enquiries,  
  surveys and research studies on various labour su bjects. 
 (ix) To conduct programmes relating to employment potential 
  of Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe candidates   
  through Coaching-cum-Guidance Centres. 
 (x) To provide amenities to workers employed in th e mining  
  industry and beedi manufacturing. 
 (xi) To assist in rehabilitation of bonded labour.  
 (xii) To provide welfare measures for certain sect ions of the  
  unorganized labour. 
 (xiii) To undertake training, education, research and   
  consultancy service in the field of industrial re lations and 
  labour in general. 
 (xiv) To educate all sections of workers for their  intelligent  
  participation in social and economic development of the  
  nation. 
 (xv) To monitor running of social security schemes  viz.   
  Employees’ Provident Fund Organization and Employ ees’  
  State Insurance Corporation. 
 (xvi) Policy framework for National Employment Ser vice,   
  Implementation of National Vocational Training   
  Programme.

 (xvii)  To mediate in industrial complaints/disput es and   
  ensure industrial peace 
 (xviii) To enforce various labour laws, thereby en suring welfare 
  of the workers 
 (xix) To provide relief and due benefits to labour ers through  
  judicial work 
 (xx) To ensure education, rehabilitation and other  welfare of  
  released child labourers through National Child L abour  
  Project 
 (xxi) To undertake survey and research work under various  
  labour laws 
 (xxii) To generate revenue for the state by receiv ing registration 
  fee under different labour laws. 
 
  The Ministry is also responsible for laying down policies in 
respect  of labour related matters including indust rial relations, 
co-operation between labour and management, settlement of labour 
disputes, regulation of wages and other conditions of work and 
safety,  women  labour  and  child  labour,  labour   welfare, social

informed that two similar insurance schemes — Aam A admi Bima

crore.  In addition to this, an amount of Rs.118.56  crore was 
provided by Ministry of  Finance from their Nationa l Social 
Security Fund.  Thus, the total allocation availabl e during 
2012-13 adds up to Rs.2588.56 crore [Rs.2470 crore + 
Rs.118.56 crore].  However, this was subsequently d ecreased to 
Rs.2118.56 crore at the RE stage but surprisingly, the Ministry 
could expend only Rs.1702.89 crore. Similarly, duri ng the year 
2013-14, an allocation of Rs.2524.00 crore includin g civil 
works component of Rs.77.90 crore was made which wa s again 
reduced to Rs.1700.00 crore at the RE stage whereas the actual 
expenditure  was Rs.1597.51 crore. The Committee ob serve 
that there has been under-spending consecutively du ring the 
12 th  Five Year Plan.  The Committee note from the alloc ation 
made by the Planning Commission each year that it i s the 

23 
 
Ministry of Labour & Employment who are not able to  utilize 
the allocation even to the extent of 50% as a resul t Planning 
Commission had to revise it downwards at the RE sta ge down 
to the level of last year’s spending.  Taking note of the 
spending for the year 2013-14 which decreased to 15 97.51 
crore, the Committee desire that the implementation  
machinery be strengthened so as to utilize the allo cated funds 
to the maximum extent possible. 
 
2.  The Committee note that the Government have tak en 
several steps to ease the procedural complexities i n 
implementation of various schemes/programmes run by  them 
viz. de-duplication, collection and collation of data, digitization 
etc.  Appreciating the steps taken by the Ministry,  the 
Committee, desire that they may be apprised, in due  course, of 
the impact of these measures in improving the servi ce delivery 
and in smooth and efficient implementation of vario us 
schemes/programmes of the Ministry.   
 
3.  The Committee find that there has been under-
utilisation of funds under the sub-Heads of (i) Soc ial Security 
for Unorganised Sector Workers Scheme; upto 35% (ii ) Skill 
Development Initiative; upto 78%and (iii) World Ban k Assisted 
Vocational Training upto 99.9%, etc. due to requirement of less 

24 
 
funds towards Central share to the State Governments and non-
receipt of utilization certificates.  The Committee  were 
informed that a policy decision has been taken to r elease the 
funds for implementation of Centrally Sponsored Sch emes to 
State Governments. The Committee observe that non/u nder-
utilisation of funds meant for Schemes is a common feature in 
some of the States which defeats the very purpose o f these 
schemes as intended benefits do not reach to the target groups.  
The Committee also feel that one of the reasons for  under-
utilisation of funds could be shortage of manpower in States.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Government to 
re-visit the decision so that atleast a strong inst itutional 
mechanism is put in place to ensure that the funds are not 
diverted nor under-utilised by the State Governments. 
 
4.  The Committee note that the Rashtriya Swasthya 
Bima Yojana (RSBY) which provides smart card based cashless 
health insurance cover of Rs.30,000/- p.a. on famil y floater 
basis to the workers of un-organised sector became operational 
w.e.f. 1
st  April, 2008.  The Committee also note that till 30 th  
April 2014, 3.71 crore smartcards had been issued t o the 
beneficiaries spread over 28 States/UTs. The Commit tee were 
also informed that the Labour Ministry has also bee n working 
on a two-phase revamp of the RSBY to make it more 
transparent and accountable with third-party audits  and a call 

25 
 
centre for grievances.  Further, according to the M inistry Aam 
Aadmi Bima Yojana and Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension 
Scheme are also proposed to be merged with RSBY.  H owever, 
despite handling, implementing and running RSBY  so  well by 
the Ministry, this Scheme is reportedly proposed to  be 
transferred to the Ministry of Health and Family We lfare for 
implementation.  The Committee are unaware of any p lausible 
logic over this decision and feel that it may not b e in the best  
interest of the poor workers as the welfare of this  class could 
be better safeguarded by the Ministry of Labour tha n by the 
Ministry of Health.    The Committee strongly feel that the 
RSBY must stay with the Ministry of Labour & Employ ment 
only. 
 
5.  The Committee take note of the global crusade 
against the use of tobacco and its harmful effects.  The workers 
engaged in beedi making/industry often succumb to i ll effects 
of tobacco and need be provided with alternative em ployable 
skills which they fit in, according to their age, q ualification, 
status, health and financial conditions.  The Commi ttee desire 
that the Ministry should explore other avenues and 
possibilities to save not only the existing workers , who wish to 
quit this profession, but also the next generation of beedi 
workers dissuading them from taking up this profess ion.  The 

26 
 
Committee desire that such workers may also be assi sted 
financially or technically to find alternative employment. 
 
6.  The Committee were informed that there are 21 
Vocational Rehabilitation Centres (VRCs) all over I ndia for 
providing vocational training to eligible persons w ith disability 
(PwD) to train them in the trades of local need.  H owever, 
keeping in view the number of PwD vis-à-vis the num ber of 
available VRCs, the Committee find the numbers extr emely 
inadequate to meet the present and future demand.   The 
Committee are, therefore, of the considered view th at there is 
an immediate need to establish more VRCs, atleast o ne in each 
State/UT for the present  and further the number of  VRCs be 
gradually increased considering the population and area of 
States. 
  
7.  The Committee view that progress/improvement of  
any scheme depends upon their critical appraisal pe riodically.  
The Committee find that evaluation/review of the sc hemes is 
done by the Planning Commission/NSSO.  The Committe e 
desire that all evaluation review of Schemes undert aken by the 
Planning Commission/NSSO in respect of Labour Burea u/VV 
Giri National Labour Institute, CVWE, Child Labour and DGE&T 

27 
 
be submitted to the Committee alongwith the corrective action 
taken by the Government. 
 
8.  The Committee find that there are nearly 118 
vacancies in DGFASLI, out of which some vacancies d ate back 
to the year 1992. The Committee are of the consider ed view 
that the existing manpower strength of DGFASLI is f ar from 
adequate to carry forward effectively and efficient ly the core 
activities of the organization.  As per information  submitted by 
the Ministry, the activities in disciplines like In dustrial 
Physiology, Ergonomics, Industrial Psychology, etc.  have come 
to a standstill.  The Committee also note that an e valuation 
study of DGFASLI was also undertaken by IIT Roorkee  in the 
year 2012 to assess the required manpower.  One of the major 
recommendations of the study was to increase the nu mber of 
posts to 735 from 358 (recommended by Staff Inspect ion Unit 
in the year 2009).    The Committee feel that the D GFASLI has 
a crucial role especially when the Government have proposed 
so many amendments in ‘The Factories Act, 1948’.  H owever, 
with the existing strength, DGFASLI cannot do justice either to 
the work in hand or to the impending work in the li ght of the 
amendments to the Factories Act. The Committee, the refore, 
desire that not only the existing vacancies be fill ed up without 
further delay but also immediate follow up action b e taken on 
the study conducted by IIT Roorkee.  The Committee also 

28 
 
desire that pending the filling up of vacancies by the UPSC, in 
the meantime, some via media be explored for fillin g up of 
these vacancies as a temporary measure, so that the  work of 
the organization is not hampered. 
 
9.  The Committee note that DGFASLI is engaged in 
conducting training programmes/ workshops/ seminars / 
conferences, etc. for professional delegates/manage ment 
representatives from industries within and outside India and 
also for the government officials.  The Committee o bserve that 
the recommendations of IIT Roorkee for upgradation of 
infrastructure facilities in DGFASLI besides enhanc ing the 
manpower, needs immediate action so as to bring the  
organization at par with the peer group all over th e World.  
They, therefore, desire that the major recommendati ons of IIT 
Roorkee, wherever feasible, be implemented without further 
delay. 
 
10.  The Committee note that DGFASLI conduct 
Seminars, Workshops, Training Programmes and Apprec iation 
and Promotional Programmes for creating awareness o n 
Occupational Safety and Health in factories and doc ks.  
However, DGFASLI does not obtain any feedback or as sessment 
from trainees on the impact of the training provide d to them. 

29 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that feedback m ust be 
obtained from the trainees/organizations sending th eir officers 
for training in DGFASLI as it will immensely help i n 
restructuring/modifying the training pattern in the  changing 
scenario eventually making DGFASLI as a pioneering 
organization in the field.

A. Policy on compassionate appointments 
(Recommendation Para No. 49) 
 
4. In their earlier Repor t, the Committee had noted that a new policy was 
introduced by RSP in 1992 which did not incorporate the provisions of earlier 
policy for compassionate appointments on the ground of death due to illness 
and in 1995 when the Trade Unions approached the Management, death due 
to three diseases was made eligible for compassionate appointment w.e.f. 
1.1.1996. The Committee were unable to comprehend the rationale behind the 
approach of the Management to follow and agree with the Trade Union(s) 
without doing any  research in the matter and  taking into consideration  the 
prevalent best practices.   The Committee further found that in 1998, the 
inclusion of  the above three diseases were given retrospective effect from 1992 
which aggravated the wrong by ratifying the discrimination done in 1996. 
 
5. In their Action Taken Note, the Ministry of Steel have stated as follows: 
“SAIL introduced the 'Employee Family Benefit Scheme (EFBS) ' with 
effect from 01.01.1989 in order to help the family to overcome the urgent 
financial crisis arising out of the death/permanent total disablement of 
the income-earning member of the family. This Scheme is applicable in 
case of death/permanent total dis ablement of an employee while in 
service and  provides for monthly payment  equivalent to last drawn Basic 
Pay and DA of the deceased/total  permanently disabled employee to 
the ex -employee/his dependent till notional date of superannuation of 
the ex -employee, subject to depositing an amount equal to PF and 
gratuity.   The deposited amount towards PF & Gratuity is returned 

 
thereafter.   The major objective of the scheme was to provide sustenance 
by  taking care of the  financial needs of the ex -employee or his 
dependents  till the date of notional superannuation of  the employee. 
The scheme with regard to providing employment on compassionate 
grounds to the dependant of an employee, who was removed from 
services of the company on account of natural  unfitness or on account 
of natural death was discontinued w.e.f. 21.11.1992 consequent  to 
introduction of EFBS at RSP in terms of the NJCS agreement. 
The scheme for providing compassionate employment at RSP in case of 
death on account of three listed diseases whic h was implemented  w.e.f. 
22.11.92 on the basis of a settlement made with the recognized union, in 
the presence of Asstt. Labour Commissioner -cum-Conciliation Officer, 
Government of Orissa, was an additional benefit provided by RSP on the 
basis of aspirations/suggestions/requests of the employees including the 
recognized representative union.”
